Let's be realistic - the only reason both Russia and European superpowers are fighting over Eastern Europe is because whichever country sides with either EU / NATO or Russia, it will provide its economic and military might (or its people as cannon fodder) to it. I am sceptical about superpower theory in application to todays situation, in my view it was more relevant in 19th century, less relevant in 20th, and nearly obsolete today. Moreover, IMO the russian government uses spheres of influence as a means to win their own class war and establish class solidarity via pondering to external enemies as a reason to tighten their own internal situation. Prior to Ukraine war in 2014, Russians protested their government en masse for few years and the situation for super rich was not very optimistic. War enabled russian government and their super rich cronies to step up with repression, banish internal dissent, and ensure some degree of support from the masses. Eastern Europe conquest here is not a real aim for them, but rather the means to improve their internal standing, e.g. the russian super-rich are not really fascist themselves, but rather using Fascism ideology to ensure compliance of population and preserve their status in society. As for European "superpowers", EU is not a traditional state and it does many things differently from one. One example I like is EU push for constituent states to enable decentralization of power and funding, so that local governments have more power over their tax flows and application of funds than the central government. Ukraine was too pushed through the decentralization as part of EU application process, and 2014-2021 period has seen immense modernization of rural communities and buildout of infrastructure in the regions. This is something unimaginable without EU influence -- prior to 2014 all taxation went through Kyiv, so rural communities were defunded and infrastructure was mostly obsolete. In traditional states, central government does not have any incentive to engage in decentralization, and when superpower theory was relevant, all superpowers were highly centralized and their regions were devoid from funding and power. Some legal documents and studies on how decentralization works in EU can be found here: https://www.coe.int/en/web/congress/the-charter-how-it-works Superstates, like the EU as a step towards eventual stateless society, how do you view the loss of political and economic autonomy for the members in it? For example, EU especially is a huge proponent of capitalism, and is now increasingly seeking to centralise more political power within its bureaucracy, I think here centralization means less power for constituent state governments as compared to EU government, not the regional governments as compared to constituent state government as I explained above. For me this is a good thing because it reduces amount of weapons that state government and oligarchy has to engage in a class war, including much less means to run a war with neighbouring states like russian government does. As for capitalism, I view current situation as transitional, and think that future challenges, such as global climate migration and hunger, will likely reduce role of capitalism in EU and elsewhere. When humans will need to adapt to daily food rationing, they will not have resources to prop up mega-corporations. The only problem is that mega-corporations could attempt to seize power during this transitional period, as we seen in the US where congregation of far-right authorities and business oligarchs worked to replace state authoriy with business authority via DOGE and similar efforts. The strong transnational authority such as EU Council and Commission eliminates such threat. In EU, capitalism is already very much different from US, India or China situation, due to high amount of regulations that corporations need to abide, and it's not going to reverse even if some constituent states wanted to. Note that Makhnovism and generally 19th-early 20th century libertarian efforts did not have mega-corporations to confront, so the situation was different at a time and did not require strong transnational authority in a first place. Personally, because of the Gandhi-Nehru political views that I believe in, I don't like either extremes of the left- or the right- ... because these extreme ideologies don't recognize the paradox that their ideology, while promising the most freedom actually seeks to subsume it within their politics. Take Makhnovism itself - while it encourages independent, grassroot councils, would it allow these councils to exist if they suddenly wanted to have a different political ideology that clashes with Makhnovism? No. Interestingly, the demise of libertarian struggle in Ukraine happened due to failed alliance between Makhnovists and Bolsheviks, and Makhno and his closest comrades were sceptical about such alliance, preferring to cooperate with Ukrainian socialist (Petliurist) authorities instead, like they did in the struggle for Ekaterinoslav prior to Bolshevik alliance. However, the Congress of local councils had different position and overruled Makhno's judgement, leading to the alliance, future betrayal and failure of Free Territory. I highly recommend work of Alexandre Skirda on the history of Makhnovism -- https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/alexandre-skirda-nes... , apart from the rich historical sources it brings, it also explains in detail the inner workings of Free Territory politics. You definitely should use grep wherever you can (i.e. simple, unranked term searches) to 1) exclude things you are definitely not care about 2) to include things you definitely do care about. The reason is that this is cheap and easy and it reduces the overall results you still need to dig through. And because everything else is much more expensive this is going to help reduce the amount of compute needed from that. And results are cacheable as well which helps you with repeat searches for similar things. For ranked searches, you can do more than one and combine their results. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) is a common approach to do that. A simple ranked lexical query and one or more vector searches. Can be combined to amplify results that perform well across multiple of these. RRF is really easy: for each search result, take its position in each ranked list, add 60, and divide 1 by that number. Add up those values across all lists to get the final score. Results that rank highly in multiple lists get higher scores. The magical number of 60 dampens the effect of highly ranked results biasing the outcome to much. It's not going to be a good approach for all data sets. But it works surprisingly well and it's stupidly easy to implement. For term search, expending some AI and other cleverness at indexing time to e.g. calculate categorizations is very helpful. If you can reduce your result set with some simple term searches, it might be small enough to pass to an LLM directly and skip ranked searches entirely. Using vector search as magic pixie dust is generally going to work a lot better if you can filter and combine it with a lexical search. Using e.g. a decision model at index time to calculate some categorizations and classifications is relatively cheap and easy relative to calculating vector embeddings.

ShanHaiGateway (shg) is a production-grade LLM API gateway written in Go. It hides multiple unreliable LLM upstreams behind a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint. I run it every day in front of 20+ model endpoints (Volcengine, Alibaba Bailian, GLM, SiliconFlow, ...). The problem it solves: every upstream fails differently — rate limits, sudden 403s, broken streaming, silent truncation — and I wanted one place that absorbs all of it instead of every client script inventing its own retry soup. What's inside: - SWRR load balancing with per-backend weights, health checks and circuit breaking (half-open probes, not just cooldown timers) - Session affinity keyed by conversation hash — prompt-cache friendly, since several providers discount cache hits heavily - Multi-tier quota tracking: daily / per-plan monthly token budgets with burn-rate forecasting (it warns you hours before a plan resets, not after you hit the wall) - Storage-vs-egress masking split: request bodies are masked aggressively before anything is persisted (keys, intranet IPs, phone numbers), while egress masking is opt-in per backend — untrusted upstreams get scrubbed, trusted paid backends get raw bytes. Masking code-shaped content breaks model edits, so the egress pattern set is deliberately narrower than the storage one - Streaming-safe failover (SSE re-splicing mid-stream), response capture ring buffer for post-mortems, a shadow ledger that records every attempt MIT licensed, single Go binary, no dependencies. Docs: https://github.com/ffseika0304/shanhai-gateway/blob/master/R... Happy to answer questions about the design — especially the masking split, which took a few production incidents to get right.

On one hand, I like the idea of being 100% responsible for reviewing my own code because it allows me to get changes in quicker. The way we've been working is that we own a feature end-to-end rather than just a slice of it. So I understand my work, and other people understand theirs. In that context, not having code reviews makes some sense. But part of me already misses what code reviews used to bring: learning opportunities. I can no longer rely on someone more senior than me to give me feedback, challenge my decisions, or help develop a shared understanding of the codebase. «I can say to Claude "hey, bring me up to speed on this thing they've been building - how does it work, where is it at, and what still needs to be done?"» I think there's an opportunity to solve this differently. If you could see your teammates' conversations with their agents, you could actually follow the decisions they made and understand why. Although I appreciate that's a bit "big brother". «What I'm recommending instead is to still build a very strong foundation in engineering fundamentals, because that's where I think we as humans offer the most value right now.» Whilst I partly agree with this, how do you actually do it in practice? How can you possibly know what good looks like without writing good code yourself and experiencing the consequences of bad code? I've been thinking of this as a privileged point of view, particularly from engineers who've spent more of their careers working pre-AI than post-AI. You've had the benefit of years of experience developing the judgment needed to distinguish good engineering from bad engineering. You can now use AI effectively precisely because you've built that foundation. But how are newer engineers supposed to develop that same judgment, especially if their workplace operates like yours? But it's valuable to experiment with these instincts.
